title: Sold a Story S2: Hanford's right about Direct Instruction. But it's not the whole story.
author: Michelle Brown
summary: Four episodes into Season 2 of Sold a Story, Michelle Brown welcomes much of Emily Hanford's reporting on Zig Engelmann's Direct Instruction while warning against another silver bullet. She credits Hanford with three things: insisting on adult accountability for whether kids learn, showing the meticulous craft of building an effective lesson, and treating instructional time as a critical resource. She then raises two concerns. The first is conflating disciplines, since the science of teaching English language arts differs from teaching advanced mathematics and the pedagogical content knowledge involved is subject-specific. The second is that the series focuses on how we teach more than what we teach, even though too many students receive thin, low-demand materials. Her conclusion is that better outcomes need discipline-specific solutions that pair effective instruction with knowledge-rich curriculum, and that the lesson of Season 1, that phonics is essential but not the whole solution, applies again.
points: Brown backs Hanford on adult accountability: with about 15,000 hours from kindergarten through grade 12, failure to learn to read is a responsibility of the school, not of external factors.

Engelmann's team piloted, debriefed and retyped lessons daily, a standard of respect for student time that today's overstuffed, commercially driven curricula rarely meet, with RAND finding teachers work about 15 hours a week beyond their contracts, 12 of them unpaid.
Middle and high schoolers get roughly eight minutes of reading a day, so instructional minutes are a scarce resource that needs deliberate use.
Treating scripted Direct Instruction as a universal fix risks mandates and large purchases that confuse a kindergarten phonics lesson with an 11th-grade argumentative essay.
Delivery cannot rescue weak content: TNTP found students succeeded on assignments 71 percent of the time but showed grade-level mastery only 17 percent of the time.
quotes: Kids spend roughly 15,000 hours in school from kindergarten through 12th grade. That’s ample time to teach them to read, regardless of their background. If students aren’t making progress, that’s on us. Period.
They scrutinized every turn of phrase, every line—and believed students had something to teach them about the lessons. It’s a level of respect for a child’s time that is breathtaking and rare.
We’re asking teachers to be both the astronauts in the spaceship and mission control at the same time.
The science of teaching English Language Arts is not the same as the science of teaching advanced mathematics.

If Season 2’s takeaway becomes “scripted Direct Instruction, everywhere,” we could see mandates and million-dollar purchases that treat a kindergarten phonics lesson and an 11th-grade argumentative essay as the same problem.
The delivery method, or the how of teaching, is only half the equation. What we teach matters just as much, if not more.

You can deliver a weak lesson perfectly. You can script it, structure it, and execute it exactly as intended. But if the content is inaccurate, intellectually shallow, or nowhere near grade level, better delivery won’t fix it.
We need discipline-specific solutions that bring together effective instruction and knowledge-rich, high-quality curriculum.

The second is that the series focuses on how we teach more than what we teach, even though too many students receive thin, low-demand materials.
